claims.text: Conventionally processed HfNbTaTiZr contains compositional variations and microstructural heterogeneity.
Microstructural regions in conventionally processed HfNbTaTiZr have localized differences in thermal expansion coefficient.
A high-temperature homogenization treatment followed by controlled slow cooling will reduce compositional and microstructural heterogeneity in HfNbTaTiZr.
Homogenization will produce a more uniform HfNbTaTiZr microstructure with smaller compositional gradients.
Homogenization will minimize differences in thermal expansion coefficient between microstructural regions.
Differences in thermal expansion behavior can generate internal tensile stresses during temperature changes or solidification.
Thermal-expansion mismatch between regions of HfNbTaTiZr is a governing cause of its unresolved thermoelastic and stress–strain behavior.
Internal thermal stresses caused by heterogeneity exacerbate high-temperature creep deformation in HfNbTaTiZr.
Internal thermal stresses caused by heterogeneity produce irregular thermoelastic responses in HfNbTaTiZr.
Reducing thermal-expansion mismatch will lower internal thermal stresses in HfNbTaTiZr.
Relative to a conventionally processed baseline, homogenized HfNbTaTiZr will show more consistent stress–strain curves.
Relative to the baseline, homogenized HfNbTaTiZr will show lower variability in elastic modulus between 293 and 1100 K.
Relative to the baseline, homogenized HfNbTaTiZr will have a lower tensile creep rate at about 1250 °C.
The predicted improvements should be observable around 1250 °C for creep and between 293 and 1100 K for elastic properties.
Aging in the 600–800 °C range is relevant to the proposed response because hardening phenomena occur in that range.
Secondary-phase formation may influence the mechanical behavior measured after heat treatment.
The cited aging study attributes high strength after aging at 700 °C for 4 h to a high density of fine L12 precipitates enabled by low lattice misfit and slow diffusion.

Failure of the homogenized specimens to reduce thermal-expansion mismatch, improve thermoelastic uniformity, and improve creep resistance relative to the conventional specimens would falsify the hypothesis.
